newsitem.title: FRANCE: Air France head still hopes for privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Air France head still hopes for privatisation.

text.p: Air France chairman Christian Blanc is hopeful he can convince the new French Socialist government to privatise the airline, despite a Communist transport minister hostile to state sell-offs.
"Christian Blanc is serene. He thinks that he can convince the government on the privatisation of Air France," a spokeswoman for the flagcarrier said on Sunday.

Jean-Claude Gayssot, the newly-appointed transport minister, told French radio on Friday: "Nobody expects Gayssot will become the minister for privatisation, deregulation and ultra-liberalism...I believe there is a role for the public service".

Blanc has long been eager to free Air France from what he sees as the dead hand of state control and run it as a "normal" commercial company. He has said he hopes for a privatisation later this year or early in 1998.

One of Blanc's proposals would involve selling 30 percent stakes in the airline to employees and the state, and five percent to each of its U.S. alliance partners, Delta Air Lines and Continental, the spokeswoman said.
The size of the stakes for the U.S. carriers has not been finalised, she stressed. The French and U.S. companies would exchange shares in each other's capital.

An aerospace executive said if Blanc could persuade the government to accept a partial privatisation of Air France, it would serve as a model for opening up the capital of defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF and France Telecom, two other companies slated for privatisation.
Blanc has not yet met the transport minister and no meeting has so far been arranged, the spokeswoman said.

Air France posted a net profit for 1997 of 394 million francs ($67.7 million), its first since 1989, despite the loss of 250 million francs from strikes. The return to the black was essential to preparing the airline for privatisation.
That recovery was made possible by 20 billion francs in state aid, used to repay debt, and which was approved by the European Commission in return for a restructuring plan and eventual privatisation.

The SNPL pilots union, which represents the majority of Air France's pilots, is considered to be positive to a privatisation. An employee shareholder scheme formed part of a recent compromise struck between management and flight crews over a controversial two-tier pay scale.

Cigar-smoking Blanc is closely identified with the left and insisted on reporting directly to former conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe rather than to his erstwhile boss, transport minister Bernard Pons. ($ = 5.818 French Francs)
